records.content: News Sports Politics Outdoors Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals OREGON Oregon matches record for bats testing positive with rabies Makenzie Stamets Salem Statesman Journal Aug. 1, 2026, 4:02 a.m. PT After 22 Oregon bats have tested positive for rabies in 2026, Oregon Health Authority and the Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife are reminding people how to prevent exposure risk. The primary way people can stay safe is to not touch dead or dying animals, officials said. Also, to keep pets away. Oregon has matched its record for bats that tested positive for rabies in a year, OHA said. Bats are the primary animal to expose humans to the virus in the U.S. Though people might want to help a dead or dying bat, more contact with bats increased rabies exposure risk, OHA’s Public Health Division veterinarian Emilio DeBess said. “When a bat or other wild animal is sick or dying with rabies, there’s an increased chance they will bite or transmit the virus in other ways," DeBess said. Bats and other wildlife rarely bite people, but might if they are sick or threatened, ODFW state wildlife veterinarian Colin Gillin said. "Bats provide important ecosystem services in Oregon, but also globally with insect control, seed dispersal, and pollination of specific plants, supporting agriculture and forest systems,” Gillin said. “And like many animals that can carry disease, bats can also prevent or suppress disease by reducing mosquitoes and other vectors that carry human and animal pathogens.” What to do if you come across a bat Since bats are protected wildlife, and it is illegal to harm or keep them. ODFW and OHA provided the following list of tips if you see a sick bat: Stay calm, do not touch it. Keep people and pets away. If the sick or dead bat is indoors, do not release it. It may have exposed someone or a pet to rabies. Place a container or box over the bat if it's safe. If the sick or dead bat is outdoors and may have exposed someone to rabies, cover it with a box or bucket to keep it in place. But, leave the bat alone unless someone was bitten or scratched before it died. Immediately report if a person or pet has been bitten or scratched by an animal that may have rabies to local animal regulation services or local public health authority. Seek medical care immediately from a medical provider or veterinarian. If multiple sick or dead bats are observed in an area report to ODFW. Avoid bats seen in the wild, such as while hiking. Teach children to avoid all contact with bats and other wildlife. Update dog or cat vaccinations, whether they are indoor or outdoor pets. Unvaccinated pets that come into contact with a bat may be quarantined for up to four months, or euthanized. Protect your home from bats by covering vents, chimneys, and other entry points with screens. If roosting bats are living in the attic, call a wildlife control operator, not ODFW. More information about rabies and bats is avaliable at OHA’s bats and rabies website and ODFW’s bats website. Makenzie Stamets is an outdoor intern at the Statesman Journal. Any person or animal that touched or had contact with the bat or its saliva could be at risk of getting rabies. If you see a bat, don’t touch it! A disproportionate number of people in jails and prisons have chronic medical or behavioral health conditions. When people leave jail, it’s a unique moment to connect them to services in the community that they may not have known about before. Maliha, a social worker in the Jail Health Release Program, shares about what she does to help people with a range of health conditions as they transition out of incarceration. Anyone who might have had physical contact with this bat (even if not bitten) could be at risk and should seek medical evaluation immediately or call Public Health at 206-296-4774 to determine if rabies preventative treatment is necessary.
